flashcards.a: A creational pattern that creates new objects by copying an existing object (the prototype) instead of constructing from scratch.

flashcards.q: What core problem does Prototype solve?
flashcards.a: It avoids expensive or complex construction when a copy of an existing object is sufficient, and lets you add product types at runtime by registering prototypes.

flashcards.q: What are the main participants in the Prototype pattern?
flashcards.a: 1) Prototype (interface with clone()), 2) ConcretePrototype (implements clone()), 3) Client (creates objects by cloning a prototype).

flashcards.q: How does Prototype differ from Factory Method?
flashcards.a: Factory Method creates objects by calling constructors or factory methods. Prototype creates objects by cloning an existing prototype.

flashcards.q: How does Prototype differ from Builder?
flashcards.a: Builder constructs an object step-by-step. Prototype creates a copy in one shot by cloning an existing object.
Copies the object and its direct fields; nested objects are shared (same references). Faster but mutating nested state affects both original and clone.
Recursively copies all nested objects so the clone is fully independent. Slower and more allocation, but no shared mutable state.
When construction is more expensive than copying, when you want to add product types at runtime, or when you need copies with small variations.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use Prototype?
flashcards.a: When objects are simple and cheap to construct, when identity matters (single canonical instance), or when deep clone is impractical (e.g. circular refs).

flashcards.q: What is a registry of prototypes?
flashcards.a: A map/store of named prototypes; the client looks up a prototype by key and then clones it to create new instances—add new types at runtime by registering new prototypes.

flashcards.q: What risk does shallow copy introduce?
flashcards.a: Mutating a nested object affects both the original and the clone, since they share the same references for nested data.

flashcards.q: Name 3 common real-world uses for Prototype.
flashcards.a: 1) Avoiding costly construction (e.g. object from DB), 2) Undo/redo or snapshots, 3) Duplicating game entities or document nodes.

flashcards.q: What is a main disadvantage of the Prototype pattern?
flashcards.a: Implementing clone correctly can be tricky: deep clone with circular references, and deciding shallow vs deep semantics.

flashcards.q: How can Prototype be combined with Abstract Factory?
flashcards.a: The factory can store or return a prototype for each product in a family; clients clone the prototype instead of the factory constructing from scratch.

flashcards.q: Why might cloning be better than construction in some cases?
flashcards.a: When the object was expensive to create (e.g. loaded from DB, heavy computation), copying its state can be cheaper than rebuilding it from scratch.
